channel.title: Nish’s Daily
channel.description: A daily front page: AI, dev, product and startup news, with the day's best stories checked against their sources.

item.title: Nish’s Daily · 2026-10-16
item.description:
I opened 11 of the 435 candidate pages and kept 7. Meta's Muse Spark Open runs on Meta's own blog rather than a rewrite, and Anthropic's investor numbers come from Simon Willison reading the Financial Times. OpenAI's newsroom blocked three stories and Reddit rate-limited three subreddits, so those lanes are thin. Nothing beat yesterday's Modal round on evidence, so demand signals is one item.

Anthropic told investors its quarterly revenue hit $16.8 billion, up nearly 50 percent, ahead of an IPO

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude family of AI models, held an investor day on Wednesday and gave three quarters of revenue numbers for the first time. Revenue went from about $4.8 billion in the first quarter to $11.5 billion in the second and $16.8 billion in the third. That is the clearest public picture yet of how fast money is moving into AI models. The company also stopped quoting a flattering yearly figure and started quoting the actual quarter, which is a harder number to spin.

Checked Anthropic told investors quarterly revenue was about $4.8 billion in Q1, $11.5 billion in Q2 and $16.8 billion in Q3 2026, with adjusted operating margins of 11 percent.

Nish Three quarters, revenue up more than three times. This is the number I keep coming back to when someone tells me AI is a bubble. At this size the question is which lab keeps that spend, so I would build assuming the model suppliers get squeezed.

But These are figures Anthropic told investors, reported by people with knowledge of the matter, and the full accounts are not public. A third quarter figure of $16.8 billion also assumes the growth held, and it did not tell us profit.

Amazon's Bee launched two personal AI devices, a $74.99 wrist band and a $99.99 phone magnet

Bee, the note-taking hardware Amazon bought last year, put out its first new gadgets. The Frontier is a band you can wear on your wrist or pin to a shirt for $74.99, and the Eclipse is a credit-card-sized slab that sticks to the back of your phone for $99.99. Both listen to the conversations around you and turn them into notes, reminders and to-do lists. That puts Amazon directly against the Plaud Note at $159 and the Pocket at $129, at roughly half the price.

Checked The Bee Frontier costs $74.99 and the Bee Eclipse $99.99, against $159 for the Plaud Note and $129 for the Pocket, and Bee Pro costs $11.99 a month.

Nish Amazon entering at half the price of everyone else tells me this category is about to get crowded and cheap. The $11.99 a month for unlimited summaries is the part I would copy, because the subscription is where the business lives.

But Amazon is selling these devices, so the privacy description is the company's own: it says the raw audio is deleted after processing and transcripts are locked with a key the device makes. I did not test that.

Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model that runs on two Mac Studios

Meta, which makes Facebook and Instagram, published the weights inside a new model it calls the most capable open-weight one built in the United States. Open-weight means the model's inner numbers are published, so anyone can inspect, host or adapt it, unlike a closed model you can only reach through an API. This one handles images and text, is built for coding work and for acting as an agent that carries out tasks, and it runs on your own desk using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios.

Checked Meta's Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters with 42 billion active, a 1 million token context window, and runs locally on two M5 Ultra Mac Studios that share about 1 terabyte of memory.

Nish Meta calling this the best open model is a claim from the company that built it, so I would wait for an outside test. What I care about is that a serious lab put the weights out. That squeezes the labs charging by the token, and that is good for me.

But The benchmark claims are Meta's own. Running it locally needs a machine most people do not own, so "runs on a Mac" is not the same as cheap or easy.

Ramp raised $1.85 billion at a $60 billion valuation four months after a $44 billion round

Ramp sells software that companies use to pay for things and to track the money: expense reports, company cards, buying approvals. It raised $1.85 billion, co-led by Dragoneer, Thrive, Founders Fund and others, at a $60 billion valuation, against $44 billion four months ago. Ramp says its annualized revenue has passed $2 billion and it now has 85,000 customers, including Visa, Uber, Shopify and Notion. The interesting part is where it is heading: AI agents that spend money, and tools that watch what those agents spend.

Checked Ramp raised $1.85 billion at a $60 billion valuation four months after a $750 million round at $44 billion, and says annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, with 85,000 customers up from 70,000.

Nish Ramp went from spending controls to the place companies manage what their AI agents spend. That is a real budget line appearing, and budgets fund products. I would sell into the finance team that already signs off on every purchase.

But The revenue and customer counts are Ramp's own, and Ramp now competes with Rippling for the same finance-team money. An investor said Ramp is going after Anthropic's business, which is a plan, not a result.

Floqer's AI agents do the sales prospecting, and it says customers cut the time by up to 70 percent

Floqer, founded in 2024, sells software that keeps a company's list of prospects up to date by itself. You describe the kind of company you want to sell to, and its AI agents search the web, pull in more than 100 data sources, and build a list with contact details, checking provider after provider until they find a verified email or phone number. It keeps watching, so when someone changes jobs or their company raises money, your records update. The team says revenue grew about tenfold over the past year and it will open-source the underlying technology in early 2027.

Checked Floqer says it has passed $1.2 million in annual recurring revenue, growing roughly tenfold over the past year, with more than 1,000 customers including Perplexity, Wise and AngelList, on $2 million raised.

Nish Eight employees, over a thousand customers. I would copy this shape. It is what selling a boring job to a hated department looks like now, and that job is customer research. Watch the open-sourcing in early 2027.

But Every number is Floqer's own, given to TechCrunch ahead of its pitch on the Startup Battlefield stage, so the growth figures are pitched to investors. The 70 percent saving is a customer report, not a measured study.

Vercel sells a $30 a month pass that gives coding agents $80 of model credit

Tokens are the chunks of text a model charges you for, roughly a slice of a word. Vercel, the hosting company, has put a Token Pass into early access for its paid teams: $30 a month buys $80 of credit to spend on the GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 models. It runs through Vercel's AI Gateway, the service that passes requests from an app to whichever model you pick, so a coding agent can switch between them on the same credit. When the credit runs out the requests stop, with no surprise overage bill.

Checked Vercel's Token Pass costs $30 per month for Pro teams and includes $80 in monthly credit for GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3, with Zero Data Retention on by default and no automatic overage charges when the credit runs out.

Nish I would buy this. My agents burn through draft work, summarizing and classifying, and a flat $30 with a hard stop beats per-token metering I have to watch. The hard stop with no overage wins, because a runaway agent cannot bill me at 3am.

But It is early access, limited to GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 for now, and the credit does not roll over month to month. Vercel is selling its own gateway, so it has every reason to make the flat rate look generous.

Citizen Lab caught the first confirmed zero-click spyware attack delivered through targeted ads

Normally you get spyware by clicking something. Citizen Lab, the surveillance researchers at the University of Toronto, have documented an attack that needs no click at all. Disguised as an advertising company called Discover-Tech, they bought ads that reached devices belonging to journalists at Al Jazeera, and the ad infected those devices with spyware from a vendor called Candiru the moment the ad appeared. The ad networks now carry bad ads on top of the ordinary kind, and this one was the delivery system for spying.

Checked Citizen Lab analyzed four billion Discover-Tech bidding records and found its ads were served on nearly 200,000 unique websites and apps over four months, and Google, IAB Europe and Beeswax all disconnected Discover-Tech.

Nish The lesson reaches past spyware. If an ad network can deliver an infection with zero clicks, then an ad network is an attack surface with a legal department. I would ask any ad-dependent vendor about their network, and not love the answer.

But This is one research group's disclosure, published the same day, and it is co-timed with a separate investigation by Confiant. Named parties have not responded in print yet, and legal action usually takes years.
